properties.title: Land off Exmouth Road, Ebford/Exton (freehold acreage with roadside vehicle access and river views — no planning consent)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (roadside vehicle access onto the land)
RIVER VIEWS OVER THE EXE ESTUARY
EXTON STATION IS WALKABLE — ON THE EXMOUTH–EXETER LINE
CLOSE TO WOODBURY AND WOODBURY COMMON
NO PLANNING PERMISSION — NOT A BUILDING PLOT AS IT STANDS
30% PLANNING OVERAGE — SELLER TAKES 30% OF ANY UPLIFT
SOLD BY A COMPANY ASSOCIATED WITH THE AGENT
LISTED SIZE CONTRADICTS ITSELF — 3.5 ACRES OR 24.7?
NO BUILDING, NO SERVICES, NOTHING TO LIVE IN

properties.body: Freehold land between the villages of Ebford and Exton, on the western edge of the Exe estuary, advertised with river views, a prominent roadside position and established vehicle access. The agent describes it as "three and a half acres" in the write-up and "over three and a half acres" in the key features, but Rightmove’s own size field for the same listing records 24.71 acres / 10 hectares — the two do not agree and the actual extent needs establishing from the title plan before anything else. The land is sold freehold subject to a 30% planning overage, meaning that if consent is ever granted the seller takes 30% of the uplift in value. The agent also states plainly that "the property is being sold by a company associated with the Signature Property Concierge", and the same seller has two further parcels on the same road at £300,000 (6 acres) and £125,000. There is no planning permission, no building and no services — it is marketed as being "ideal for a variety of uses subject to the necessary consents".
properties.why: Bare land is explicitly on your list — self-build plots are one of the unconventional routes you asked to be shown — and on the face of it this is cheap freehold acreage, well under your £170k target, in a genuinely good spot: Exton station is on the Exmouth–Exeter line within walking distance, Woodbury and the Common are a few minutes away, and it looks over the estuary. It is on the list for that reason. But it needs flagging hard rather than sold to you. There is no planning permission, so it is not a building plot — it is a field, and East Devon’s green-field policy makes residential consent between two small villages a long shot rather than a formality. The 30% overage means that even if you did win consent, the seller takes nearly a third of the gain you created. The seller being a company associated with the selling agent, based in Hampshire, marketing several roadside parcels at once with overage attached, matches the shape of land-banking sales, where buyers pay a premium over agricultural value for land whose consent never arrives. And the listing cannot agree with itself on whether you are buying 3.5 acres or 24.7. Treat this as a speculative punt to investigate with a solicitor and a look at East Devon’s local plan, not as a plot to build on.

parking.note: Not a home, so parking in the ordinary sense does not apply — but the listing’s main selling point is a prominent roadside position on Exmouth Road with established vehicle access, so you can get a vehicle onto the land itself. Flagged here as "has" purely so the entry carries an explicit parking status like every other property on the page.

checklist.uniqueFeature: Freehold acreage on the estuary edge with its own roadside vehicle access and a station walkable from it — but no consent, and a 30% overage clawback attached

properties.aiTake: Cheap freehold acreage in a genuinely good position — estuary views, Exton station walkable, Woodbury Common close — but with no planning consent, a 30% overage clawback, a seller connected to the agent, and a listing that contradicts itself on the acreage, it is a speculative punt rather than somewhere you could build.

properties.title: Jarvis Close, Exmouth (2 double bedroom semi-detached bungalow, driveway and garage, no chain)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (driveway plus garage with remote door)
GARAGE WITH POWER AND LIGHT — USABLE AS A WORKSHOP
TWO DOUBLE BEDROOMS, BOTH WITH BUILT-IN WARDROBES
ELECTRIC HEATERS ONLY — NO GAS CENTRAL HEATING
£290,000 — NEAR THE TOP OF THE BUDGET

properties.body: A spacious two double bedroom semi-detached bungalow tucked away in a quiet close, close to bus services, shops and a post office, and offered with no onward chain. The double-glazed accommodation comprises an entrance hallway with a loft hatch and pull-down ladder, a 15’7" x 13’2" lounge/dining room opening into a study/snug, a kitchen with a range of base and eye-level units and plumbing for a washing machine, two double bedrooms (11’10" x 11’3" and 11’10" x 8’11") both with built-in double wardrobes and sliding patio doors onto the rear garden, and a shower room/WC with a quadrant cubicle and Mira shower. Outside, the front garden is laid to faux grass for ease of maintenance with an outside tap, a driveway provides off-road parking and leads to a 16’1" x 8’5" garage with a remote-operated up-and-over door, power, light and a courtesy door into the rear garden. The rear garden is laid mainly to stone paving with flower and shrub borders. Freehold, Council Tax Band C. Heating is by electric heaters with an Ariston electric water heater — there is no gas central heating.
properties.why: This is the practical end of the search rather than the romantic one. It is the single best answer on the list to the "could I still live here if I could not manage stairs" question — a true bungalow, everything on one level, with a level walk to shops and buses — and it comes with the things most of the cheap characterful cottages cannot offer: its own driveway, a proper garage with power and light that would work as a workshop, gardens front and rear, and freehold with no chain. What you are giving up is character: it is a plain post-war bungalow in a close, with nothing period about it, and it is the opposite of remote. The running-cost catch is real too — electric heaters and an electric water heater rather than gas central heating will cost noticeably more to run, and that is worth pricing in. At £290,000 it is close to the ceiling and a long way over your £170k target.

parking.note: A private driveway giving off-road parking, leading to a 16’1" x 8’5" garage with a remote-operated up-and-over door, power and light, and a courtesy door through to the rear garden. This is the strongest parking of any entry added this sweep — nothing to research.

properties.aiTake: The most practical entry on the list — a genuine one-level bungalow with its own driveway, a powered garage/workshop, gardens both sides, freehold and no chain — but completely without character, on electric-only heating, and at £290,000 near the top of what you would pay.

properties.title: Helena Place, Exmouth (19th-century workers’ cottage, freehold, renovation project, downstairs bathroom already in)

flags.text: BATHROOM IS ALREADY ON THE GROUND FLOOR
CENTRAL EXMOUTH — WALK TO BEACH, STATION AND SHOPS
FRONT GARDEN AND PRIVATE REAR COURTYARD
COUNCIL TAX BAND A — THE CHEAPEST BAND
ON-STREET PARKING ONLY (council permit — no space of its own)
MID-TERRACE IN A CENTRAL STREET — NOT REMOTE OR PRIVATE

properties.body: A 19th-century terraced workers’ cottage in the heart of Exmouth, sold as a renovation project and priced with the work in mind. The ground floor runs from an entrance porch into a generous reception room with both front and rear aspects and a gas fireplace, then through to a galley-style kitchen and a tiled bathroom fitted with WC, wash basin, short bath and overhead shower. Upstairs are two well-proportioned double bedrooms. Outside there is a front garden and a private rear courtyard. A permit parking space is available through East Devon District Council. Offered with no onward chain. Freehold, Council Tax Band A, EPC rating D.
properties.why: At £160,000 this is one of the few genuinely characterful freehold houses on the whole list that sits under your real £170k target rather than the £300k ceiling — and it is a house, not a flat, with no service charge, no ground rent and the cheapest council tax band. The workers’-cottage origin gives it real character, and there is a quietly important practical detail: the bathroom is already on the ground floor alongside a large reception room, which makes single-level living far more achievable here than in most two-up-two-down cottages, where the only bathroom is upstairs. Against that, it is priced low because it needs the work — budget for the renovation on top, the way Bro 3 always does — and it is a mid-terrace in a central street, which is the opposite of the remote/rural setting you have said you would prefer. Parking is a permit rather than a space of your own.

parking.note: No drive or garage — the agent says only that “a permit parking space is available through East Devon District Council”. Two separate schemes are relevant and it is worth checking which one the agent means. East Devon District Council sells car-park permits covering its own car parks: £120 a year for an annual permit, or £10 a month for one town (£2 extra per additional town, capped at £20/month) — that buys you a space in a council car park, not outside the door. Separately, Devon County Council runs the on-street residents’ permit scheme; three residents’ parking zones went live in Exmouth in 2023 (including the Albion Hill area, which is close to Helena Place) with further central zones proposed, administered through the MiPermit portal, with a maximum of two resident and two visitor permits per property depending on zone. Worth confirming with the agent and with DCC whether this address actually falls inside a residents’ zone before relying on it.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A 19th-century workers’ cottage — built for working families rather than as a villa, and it still has that small-scale original layout, including a ground-floor bathroom that most cottages of this size do not have

properties.aiTake: A freehold character cottage under your £170k target, walkable to the beach and station, band A council tax, no chain, and a ground-floor bathroom that makes long-term single-level living realistic — held back by needing a full renovation, permit-only parking, and being a central terrace rather than anywhere remote.

properties.title: Suffolk Cottage, Greenway, Woodbury (Grade II listed 17th-century cottage, freehold, log burner, three floors)

flags.text: IN WOODBURY ITSELF — SAME VILLAGE AS YOUR BROTHER
WOODBURY COMMON MTB TRAILS ON THE DOORSTEP
EXPOSED BEAMS AND A LOG BURNER
VERSATILE TOP-FLOOR ATTIC ROOM — USABLE AS A 3RD BEDROOM
FRONT PATIO GARDEN ONLY — NO REAR GARDEN
LISTED STATUS LIMITS WHAT YOU CAN CHANGE
ALL BEDROOMS AND THE BATHROOM ARE UPSTAIRS

properties.body: Suffolk Cottage is a Grade II listed cottage in the heart of Woodbury, believed to date back to the 17th century and presented in excellent condition. The front door opens into a spacious, light-filled sitting/dining room centred on a fireplace with a wood-burner and looking out over the front garden. Off it sits a well-appointed kitchen with a Belfast sink, wooden base units, integrated dishwasher, oven with gas hob and open shelving, with an adjoining utility room. Stairs rise to two well-proportioned double bedrooms, one with fitted wardrobes overlooking the garden, and a generous family bathroom with both a shower and a free-standing bath. A second flight leads to a versatile top-floor attic room, currently used as a bedroom — which is why the agent markets it as a 2/3 bedroom cottage. Outside there is an enclosed, low-maintenance front garden laid to patio that catches sun through the day, with a raised flower bed and a generous log store. 976 sq ft in total. Freehold, Council Tax Band B, mains water/electric/gas with gas central heating, and standard/superfast/ultrafast broadband available.
properties.why: This is the kind of property the search exists to find: a genuinely old, Grade II listed cottage with exposed beams and a log burner, freehold, in Woodbury itself — the same village as your brother, with Woodbury Common and its mountain bike trails effectively on the doorstep. At 976 sq ft over three floors it is bigger than most of the central-Woodbury cottages on file, and the attic room gives real flexibility. The honest catches are the ones that apply to nearly every cottage in that village core: there is no parking of your own, just on-street plus the free Flower Street car park a couple of minutes away, and the only outside space is a front patio — no rear garden at all. Listed status will also constrain what you can alter, which matters given every bedroom and the only bathroom are upstairs. At £285,000 it is well past your £170k target and towards the top of the range, so the question is whether the character and the village earn that premium over the cheaper Woodbury cottages already tracked.

parking.note: The agent lists on-street parking only — no space, drive or garage. Greenway is in the central village core, so the practical backstop is the same as for the other central-Woodbury cottages on file: Flower Street car park (EX5 1LX) is free with a 23-hours-in-24 maximum stay and is a couple of minutes’ walk, and there is a second free car park beside Woodbury Village Hall. No residents’ permit scheme operates in Woodbury, so this is unrestricted on-street plus two free car parks rather than a permit situation — workable, but you would be walking to your car.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A three-storey 17th-century cottage on a small footprint — the top-floor attic room gives a genuine third room above two full floors, which is unusual in a village terrace this size

properties.aiTake: Real 17th-century Grade II character, freehold, in your brother’s village with the Common’s trails on the doorstep and more space than most central-Woodbury cottages — but no parking, no rear garden, everything upstairs, and £285,000 is a long way past your £170k target.

properties.title: Raleigh Road, Budleigh Salterton (3-bed apartment at Raleigh Court with a private garage and sun terrace — 47-year lease)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (private garage + communal and visitor parking)
HALF A MILE FROM THE TOWN CENTRE AND SEAFRONT
MORTGAGE LIKELY DIFFICULT AT 47 YEARS — LEASE EXTENSION COST ON TOP
FIRST FLOOR VIA AN INTERNAL COMMUNAL STAIRCASE — NO LIFT
NO PETS AND NO HOLIDAY LETS PERMITTED

properties.body: A purpose-built first-floor apartment in Raleigh Court, an intimate and private development half a mile from Budleigh Salterton town centre and seafront, with fine views over the surrounding area and the Otter Estuary. The accommodation is tastefully presented and extremely light thanks to several double aspects and a southerly orientation: three bedrooms, a large living room, a kitchen/breakfast room, a bathroom and a separate WC, plus a delightful sun terrace. It comes with a private garage, and the development has attractive communal grounds with private and visitors’ parking. The agent notes the external fabric of the building and the communal gardens are in excellent condition and maintained to a very high standard, and the location is convenient for the main bus routes with easy access to the scenic Otter Estuary. Flood risk is very low, under 0.1% a year. The critical detail sits in the small print: the lease has only 47 years remaining. Ground rent is £25 a year and the maintenance charge is approximately £303.44 per quarter, covering buildings insurance, garden maintenance and cleaning and lighting of communal areas. No holiday lets and no pets are permitted. Council Tax Band D. Access is via an internal communal staircase.
properties.why: On the face of it this is good value — three bedrooms, a private garage, a sun terrace and estuary views in a well-kept private development, in budget at £250,000 and a short drive from the brother near Otterton. The 47-year lease is the problem, and it is a serious one rather than a quibble. Most mainstream lenders want considerably more than 47 years left at the point of purchase, so this is realistically a cash buy or a specialist-lender buy, and the same wall will face anyone Jesse eventually sells to. Extending it under the leasehold reforms is possible but not cheap, and below the 80-year mark marriage value has historically pushed the premium up sharply — that cost needs pricing in as part of the purchase, not treated as a later problem. Jesse has been happy with 99 and 114-year leases before; this is a different category of risk. Add that it is first floor up a communal staircase with no lift, which fails the long-term ground-floor test, and pets are barred. The garage and the setting are genuinely attractive, so it is worth a conversation with the agent about the lease extension cost — but that number decides it.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A private garage and a south-facing sun terrace looking over the Otter Estuary, in a small and unusually private development.

properties.aiTake: Three bedrooms, a private garage, a sun terrace and Otter Estuary views for £250,000 would be a good buy if not for the 47-year lease, which puts it beyond most mainstream mortgage lenders and lands an extension bill on top of the asking price.

parking.note: A private garage is included with the apartment, and the development has its own communal parking plus a dedicated visitors’ parking area — the agent lists parking availability explicitly as "communal parking and private garage". That is the strongest parking provision of anything added this sweep, and a garage also gives Jesse lockable storage or workshop space for bikes, which very little else on the list at this price offers.

properties.title: 4 The Strand, Exmouth (2 double bedrooms above a shop in the town centre, 168-year lease)

flags.text: TWO DOUBLE BEDROOMS AT THIS PRICE
PRIME CENTRAL EXMOUTH — WALK TO BEACH, STATION AND SHOPS
CASH BUYERS PREFERRED — LENDING LIKELY DIFFICULT
UP A COMMUNAL STAIRCASE — NOT GROUND FLOOR

properties.body: A generously proportioned two-double-bedroom flat set above commercial premises in an attractive traditional building right in the heart of Exmouth, on The Strand. It is approached via a communal entrance and staircase, opening into a surprisingly spacious interior. The main living area is the highlight — ample room for both lounge and dining furniture, with a bank of large windows overlooking the town and an elevated position that lets in plenty of daylight — alongside a fitted kitchen. There is an option to purchase the flat fully furnished. Tenure is a lease running from 26 October 2007 to 30 November 2194, roughly 168 years remaining, at a peppercorn ground rent, with a service charge of £480.73 per quarter. Council Tax Band B. The agent states cash buyers are preferred, with some lenders available. The position is about as central as Exmouth gets: shops, cafés and restaurants on the doorstep, the sandy beach and seafront within easy reach, Exmouth railway station convenient for services to Exeter, and Manor Gardens, Phear Park and the Exe Estuary all close by.
properties.why: Two double bedrooms in the middle of Exmouth for £140,000 with a 168-year lease and a peppercorn ground rent is a lot of space for the money, and the big windows over the town give it more personality than most flats at this price. There is a reason it is cheap, though, and the agent is upfront about it: cash buyers are preferred, which is the standard signal that flats above commercial premises are hard to mortgage — many lenders simply decline them, which limits both who can buy it now and who can buy it from you later. The service charge is close to £1,923 a year, it is up a communal staircase with no ground-floor option, no parking is mentioned, and there is no outside space at all. Best read as a cash purchase for someone who wants a big, cheap, central bolt-hole and accepts that resale will be to the same narrow pool of cash buyers.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A large flat sitting directly over a shopfront on The Strand, with a bank of windows looking out over the middle of Exmouth.

properties.aiTake: Two double bedrooms in central Exmouth for £140,000 on a 168-year peppercorn lease is real space for the money, but "cash buyers preferred" above a shopfront means a mortgage is unlikely, the service charge is nearly £2,000 a year, and there is no parking or outside space.

parking.note: Parking is not mentioned in the particulars, which for a flat over a shopfront on The Strand almost certainly means none is included. This is the busiest part of central Exmouth. Devon County Council runs the residents’ parking permit scheme covering central Exmouth through MiPermit at roughly £35 a year for a first band A permit, but the zones were set street by street and The Strand is a pedestrianised-edge retail frontage, so a residents’ permit may not be available for this address at all — this is the specific thing to check with Devon County Council before going further. Failing that, East Devon District Council sells a virtual monthly permit for its Exmouth town car parks, and Elizabeth Hall and Imperial Road car parks are the nearest options, both within a few minutes’ walk but priced for shoppers and summer visitors.

properties.title: Hartley Road, Exmouth (1-bed flat, no chain, residents’ parking)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (residents’ parking with the development)
WALKING DISTANCE TO TOWN CENTRE AND SEAFRONT
SERVICE CHARGE £1,800/YR — HEAVY AGAINST A £90,000 PRICE
ELECTRIC HEATING ONLY — NO GAS CENTRAL HEATING
FLOOR LEVEL NOT STATED IN THE PARTICULARS

properties.body: A one-bedroom flat on Hartley Road offered with no ongoing chain, within walking distance of Exmouth town centre and seafront. The accommodation runs entrance hall, lounge with a utility cupboard plumbed for a washing machine, kitchen with base and eye-level cupboards and a built-in oven and hob, a shower room with a three-piece white suite including a corner wash hand basin and WC, and a double bedroom. Double glazing throughout and electric heating. Residents’ parking comes with the development. Tenure is a 125-year lease running from 6 June 1994, leaving roughly 93 years, with ground rent of £30 every six months and a service charge of £900 every six months which includes the buildings insurance. Council Tax Band A. The particulars do not state which floor the flat is on.
properties.why: At a £90,000 guide this is among the cheapest things on the list that is a straightforward full-ownership purchase rather than a retirement lease or a shared-ownership share, and it comes with the two things cheap Exmouth flats usually lack: residents’ parking and no onward chain. A 93-year lease is fine, Council Tax Band A keeps running costs down, and the town centre and seafront are walkable. The catch is proportional rather than absolute — £1,800 a year in service charge plus £60 ground rent is a lot of money set against a £90,000 asset, and it is money you cannot get back. Electric-only heating pushes the bills up further. The particulars are also thin: they never say which floor it is on, which matters for Jesse’s long-term ground-floor test, and no garden or outside space is mentioned. Cheap enough to be worth a call to the agent to pin down the floor level and what exactly the service charge buys.
properties.aiTake: A £90,000 chain-free one-bed with residents’ parking and a 93-year lease inside walking distance of Exmouth seafront — genuinely cheap, but £1,800 a year of service charge against a £90,000 price is a heavy drag and the particulars never say which floor it is on.

parking.note: The particulars list residents’ parking as a benefit of the development, so a space comes with the flat rather than needing a council permit — a real advantage at this price point in Exmouth, where most flats under £100,000 have nothing at all. Worth confirming with the agent whether the space is specifically allocated to this flat or is first-come-first-served across the residents’ area, as the wording does not distinguish between the two.

properties.title: Manchester Road, Exmouth (two independent 1-bed flats sold as one lot — AUCTION 17 Sept)

flags.text: TWO SELF-CONTAINED FLATS IN ONE LOT
EXMOUTH TOWN CENTRE — LEVEL WALK TO STATION, MARINA AND SEAFRONT
SOLD AS AN INVESTMENT — BOTH FLATS CURRENTLY TENANTED
SPLIT TENURE — 4a FREEHOLD, 6a ON A 999-YEAR LEASE FROM 1989
ALL LIVING SPACE IS UP THE STAIRS IN BOTH FLATS

properties.body: An unusual lot going to online auction on Thursday 17 September: two entirely independent one-bedroom flats, 4a and 6a Manchester Road, sold together in the heart of Exmouth town centre. Each flat has its own private front door at ground level and then a landing, kitchen, living room, bedroom and bathroom/WC upstairs — they share nothing internally. Both are currently let: 4a on an AST at £575 pcm, 6a at £700 pcm with the tenant having served notice to leave. Tenure is split — 4 Manchester Road, including the flat known as 4a, is freehold, while 6a is held on the remainder of a 999-year lease dated from 1989 with a peppercorn ground rent. Council Tax Band A. The agent is pitching it squarely at lettings investors wanting ready-made income, or at buyers who would refurbish for onward sale once vacant possession is available. Open-day viewing slots are being run through late August and early September ahead of the auction.
properties.why: This is on the list because it is genuinely unconventional and genuinely cheap — £130,000 guide for two self-contained flats with the main title freehold, right in the middle of Exmouth on a level walk to the station, marina and seafront. There are two interesting angles: live in one and let the other to cover most of the running costs, or take the pair back into a single house once both are vacant. Be clear-eyed about what it is not, though. It is marketed as an income asset rather than a home, both flats are tenanted right now so vacant possession is not immediate, and the split tenure between a freehold and a leasehold flat makes the legal pack essential reading before bidding. Both flats put every room upstairs, which rules the lot out on Jesse’s long-term ground-floor test, there is no parking mentioned anywhere, and no floorplan has been published. Auction guide prices in Exmouth have been running over on the day, so treat £130,000 as a starting point.

checklist.uniqueFeature: Two completely independent one-bedroom flats sold as a single lot, with the main title freehold — so you can live in one and let the other, or reunite them into one house.

properties.aiTake: Two self-contained flats in central Exmouth for a £130,000 auction guide with the main title freehold — a genuinely interesting live-in-one-let-the-other play, but it is sold as a tenanted investment, all rooms are upstairs in both, and there is no parking.

parking.note: The particulars do not mention parking at all, which for a town-centre address of this type almost certainly means there is none with the property. Manchester Road sits in central Exmouth, inside the area Devon County Council covers with its residents’ parking permit scheme run through MiPermit, where a first band A permit is roughly £35 a year — cheap if this street falls inside a live zone, but the zones were drawn street by street and a permit gives priority rather than a reserved bay. East Devon District Council also sells a virtual monthly permit for its Exmouth town car parks, and the Imperial Road and Elizabeth Hall car parks are both a short level walk away. Confirm the zone for this exact address with Devon County Council before bidding, and note that a lot with two flats may generate demand for two vehicles.

properties.title: Fore Street, Budleigh Salterton (2-bed ground-floor flat at The Rolle — step-free, allocated parking, coastal path from the garden)

flags.text: STEP-FREE ENTRY — LIFT FROM THE BASEMENT
HAS PARKING (allocated space at the front + visitor parking)
COMMUNAL GARDENS OPEN STRAIGHT ONTO THE COASTAL PATH
HEART OF BUDLEIGH — YARDS FROM THE HIGH STREET AND SEAFRONT
SERVICE CHARGE ~£2,990/YR AND RISING 5% EVERY JULY

properties.body: A purpose-built ground-floor apartment in The Rolle, on the town-centre side of the building, a stone’s throw from Budleigh Salterton’s High Street and seafront. The accommodation is bright and well-proportioned with double glazing and gas-fired central heating throughout: a long entrance hall, a 15’5" x 10’4" living room, a 12’4" x 10’4" kitchen, a large 18’10" principal bedroom, a second bedroom, and a bathroom/WC that has been tastefully refurbished. The kitchen is the one room the agent admits needs updating. Unusually for a period-town flat, the property can be reached without using a single step, via the basement and lift, though there are stairs to all floors as well. Outside there is an allocated parking space at the front, ample visitor parking, basement storage, and large communal gardens to the rear that are maintained to a high standard, afford views over the beach and Lyme Bay, and open directly onto the coastal path. Tenure is a 999-year lease from October 2007 with the freehold held by Ellor Management Company Ltd, in which every flat owner holds a share. Council Tax Band D.
properties.why: This ticks an unusual number of Jesse’s practical boxes at once: genuinely all on one level, step-free from the street via the lift, a share of the freehold on a lease so long it is effectively freehold, its own allocated parking space, and a garden gate that opens onto the coastal path in the middle of Budleigh Salterton. For a two-bedroom home with parking at £220,000 in that location, that is a strong package, and it is a short hop to the brother near Otterton. The number to weigh against it is the service charge: £1,459.02 for six months, escalating 5% every July, which is close to £3,000 a year now and compounds from here — over a decade that is a serious sum against a £220,000 purchase. It is also a modern purpose-built block rather than anything with character, the kitchen needs money spent, and Council Tax Band D is high for a two-bed flat. Worth a look for the accessibility and the setting, with the service charge trajectory checked hard.

checklist.uniqueFeature: The communal garden opens directly onto the South West Coast Path, and the flat can be entered without a single step by going in through the basement and taking the lift.

properties.aiTake: Step-free two-bed with its own parking space and a garden gate onto the coastal path in the middle of Budleigh for £220,000 — practically excellent and close to the Otterton brother, but it is a characterless purpose-built block with a near-£3,000 service charge that climbs 5% a year.

parking.note: An allocated car parking space at the front of the property is included, and the development has ample additional visitors’ parking. Confirmed in the agent’s particulars — no permit or kerbside hunting required, which is a genuine advantage in central Budleigh Salterton where on-street space is heavily contested through the summer.

properties.title: 41 North Street, Exmouth (2-bed apartment walkable to the beach — heavy service charge)

flags.text: WALKING DISTANCE TO TOWN CENTRE, BEACH AND MARINA
SERVICE CHARGE £1,787.90/YR + £175 GROUND RENT — ~£1,963 A YEAR
NO FLOORPLAN AND NO FLOOR LEVEL STATED

properties.body: A two-bedroom apartment at 41 North Street in central Exmouth, marketed by an online nationwide agent. An entrance hall leads to all the principal rooms, with a spacious open-plan living, dining and kitchen area at the heart of the flat, a principal double bedroom with room for freestanding furniture, a versatile second bedroom suited to a guest room or home office, and a modern bathroom with a shower. Council tax band A. The lease is 100 years beginning 29 September 2017, leaving roughly 91 years, with ground rent of £175 a year and a service charge of £1,787.90 a year. The particulars are pitched squarely at first-time buyers and buy-to-let investors, and there is no floorplan, no statement of which floor the flat is on, and no mention of parking or outside space.
properties.why: Two bedrooms in central Exmouth for offers over £140,000 is genuinely under Jesse’s target and rare enough to be worth tracking. The problem is what comes with it. A service charge of £1,787.90 plus £175 ground rent is close to £1,963 a year, or roughly £164 a month, which on a £140,000 purchase is a heavy ongoing drag and would need explaining — that level of charge usually implies significant communal fabric, lifts or a managing agent with an expensive remit. The lease at about 91 years is comfortably above the 80-year danger line but is ticking, and extending later costs money. There is no parking and North Street is not covered by Exmouth’s residents’ permit zones, so that has to be solved with a car park season permit. And with no floorplan and no floor level stated, there is no way to test it against the ground-floor-long-term criterion at all. Cheap headline, expensive to hold — ask what the service charge actually buys before anything else.
properties.aiTake: Two bedrooms in central Exmouth under £145,000 is a rare headline, but a £1,963-a-year service charge and ground rent, no parking, and a listing with no floorplan or floor level take most of the shine off.

parking.note: No parking is offered and none is mentioned. This is the same North Street situation already researched for the other flat tracked on this street: kerbside space in central Exmouth is time-limited and enforced 8am to 6pm Monday to Saturday, and although North Street fell inside the area consulted on for Exmouth’s residents’ parking scheme, the zones that actually went live cover The Colonies, St Andrews Road, part of Albion Hill and Carter Avenue — not North Street. So there is currently no residents’ permit to buy for this address. The realistic answer is a season permit in an East Devon District Council long-stay car park: Imperial Road Recreation Ground is the main long-stay option at roughly 240 spaces and about five minutes’ walk, with the Manor Road and Magnolia car parks closer still. Given the service charge already running at nearly £2,000 a year, the cost of a car park season ticket on top is worth pricing before committing.

properties.title: Heydons Hall, Heydons Lane, Sidmouth (former school building on a central plot — lapsed consent for two houses)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (small parking area to the front on Heydon’s Lane)
CENTRAL SIDMOUTH — WALK TO THE ESPLANADE
PLANNING HAS LAPSED — 2009 CONSENT RENEWED 2012, LONG EXPIRED
BUILD OR CONVERSION COST ON TOP OF THE PURCHASE PRICE
BACKS DIRECTLY ONTO SIDMOUTH RUGBY CLUB CLUBHOUSE
NOT HABITABLE AS IT STANDS — CLASSROOM BUILDING

properties.body: A building on its own plot in the centre of Sidmouth, used for some years as classrooms by the Sidmouth International School, with a small parking area to the front on Heydon’s Lane. It previously held outline planning permission granted in April 2009 and renewed in July 2012 for demolition of the existing building and erection of a pair of semi-detached two-bedroom houses with rear gardens and parking to the front. That permission has lapsed. The agent frames three routes: carry on using the existing building as it is, try to reinstate the old permissions for two dwellings, or seek a fresh permission for a single detached house with parking. A footpath connecting Roselands to Heydon’s Lane runs to the south-west, the garden of 5 Roselands backs onto the rear, and the entire north-east boundary is the Sidmouth Rugby Club clubhouse, with the path between the two owned by the rugby club. Freehold.
properties.why: This is the unconventional end of the search — not a house but a plot with a building on it, freehold, in the middle of a Jurassic Coast town, with parking already established and a walk to the esplanade. If a fresh permission for a single detached house came through, £250,000 for a central Sidmouth plot with parking would look like a good starting number. The problem is that the planning has lapsed and has been lapsed for over a decade, so nothing here is consented — you would be buying on the strength of a 2012 precedent, not a live permission, and East Devon’s policy has moved on since. Add build costs on top and the total is well past the ceiling unless the existing building can be converted rather than replaced. Two boundary details deserve a look on site too: the rugby clubhouse runs the full length of one side, which means noise and floodlights on match days, and there is a public footpath along another. High risk, real upside, and only worth pursuing with a planning consultant’s view first.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A former international-school classroom block on its own freehold plot in central Sidmouth, sharing its entire north-east boundary with the rugby club clubhouse — buy it as a building, a conversion or a demolition-and-rebuild.

properties.aiTake: A freehold central-Sidmouth plot with parking and three possible futures for £250,000 is a real opportunity, but the planning lapsed over a decade ago, build cost sits on top, and a rugby clubhouse runs the length of one boundary.

parking.note: A small parking area sits to the front of the building on Heydon’s Lane and is part of the property, and the lapsed 2009/2012 consent for two houses also had parking to the front — so vehicular access and hardstanding are already established rather than something you would have to argue for. That matters more than usual here, because central Sidmouth parking is genuinely difficult: the nearby Mill Street car park has gone public pay-and-display and its reserved-permit list is closed. Worth measuring on site how many cars the front area actually takes.

properties.title: Byron Way, Exmouth (1-bed with its own private entrance and off-road parking space, 999-year lease)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (own off-road space to the front)
OWN PRIVATE ENTRANCE — NO COMMUNAL HALL
ALL LIVING SPACE IS UP THE STAIRS
NIGHT STORAGE HEATERS — NO CENTRAL HEATING

properties.body: A one-bedroom first-floor flat on Byron Way in north Exmouth, sold with its own private front door rather than a shared entrance. A storm porch with a storage cupboard leads to a private front door and an entrance hallway with the stairs rising to the living accommodation. The lounge is a good size at 18’0" x 14’9" narrowing to 8’8", with two double-glazed windows to the front and a further window to the side. There is an inner hallway with a coats cupboard and an airing cupboard housing the water cylinder, a 10’0" x 4’8" galley kitchen with built-in electric hob and oven and plumbing for a washing machine, a 10’0" x 8’7" double bedroom with a built-in wardrobe, and a bathroom with a bath and Mira shower over. Outside there is a parking space for one car to the front. Held on a 999-year lease from 1995 with the vendor insuring the property and external maintenance split. Heating throughout is a night storage heater in the lounge and electric wall heaters elsewhere — there is no gas central heating.
properties.why: The two things this gets right are the two things flats at this price usually get wrong: it has its own off-road parking space, and it has its own private front door rather than a communal hallway, on a lease so long it is functionally freehold. At £149,950 that is under Jesse’s real target with parking already solved, and the 18-foot lounge is a genuinely generous room for the money. Against that: every bit of the living space is up a flight of stairs, which fails the long-term single-level test outright, there is no garden, it is plain modern stock with no character, and the heating is night storage plus electric wall panels — the most expensive way to heat a flat and a running-cost problem rather than a cosmetic one. Five photographs is also thin. A practical, cheap, parked bolthole rather than anything Jesse would fall for.
properties.aiTake: Its own front door, its own parking space and a 968-year lease for under £150,000 is a genuinely practical package, undone by stairs to every room, night storage heating and no character at all.

parking.note: A parking space for one car directly to the front of the property, off-road and included in the sale. That is the single strongest thing about this flat — off-road parking with a one-bedroom flat under £150,000 is rare in Exmouth, and it removes the residents’-permit question entirely.

properties.title: Morton Road, Exmouth (ground-floor 1-bed with its own private entrance and sun-trap courtyard, share of freehold)

flags.text: OWN PRIVATE ENTRANCE — NO COMMUNAL HALL
MOMENTS FROM THE SEAFRONT AND MARINA, 5-MIN LEVEL WALK TO TOWN
VERY SMALL — 24.1 SQ M / 259 SQ FT IN TOTAL

properties.body: A stylishly finished open-plan apartment on Morton Road, moments from Exmouth seafront and marina and a five-minute level walk from the town centre. It has its own entrance at the rear of the building leading into a private courtyard that catches the sun for most of the day and has been landscaped for low maintenance. Inside is an open-plan kitchen and living space under a vaulted ceiling finished with wooden trims, with a generous modern kitchen including an integrated slimline dishwasher and a U-shaped run of worktops forming a breakfast bar; a double bedroom with built-in storage; and a modern shower room. It comes with a share of the freehold on a 992-year lease, council tax band A. The floorplan is the number to pay attention to: the whole flat is 24.1 square metres — 259 square feet — on one level, excluding the courtyard.
properties.why: For £150,000 this is a lot of the right things at once — share of freehold on a lease so long it is effectively freehold, entirely on one level, its own front door rather than a shared hallway, a private sun-trap courtyard, and a position by the marina with the town a level five-minute walk away. The finish looks genuinely good rather than landlord-grade. But 259 square feet is very small indeed: the whole flat is roughly the size of a single large room, the bedroom is 8’10" x 9’10" and the bathroom is under four feet wide. That is a real constraint rather than a quibble, and the agent’s own closing line pitching it as a holiday-rental investment tells you who it is really aimed at. Parking is kerbside only in a part of town under heavy summer pressure. Worth seeing if the location and the private courtyard outweigh the footprint — but go and stand in it before deciding.

checklist.uniqueFeature: Its own private street-level entrance and enclosed courtyard, in a seafront-adjacent block where almost everything else at this price shares a communal hall.

properties.aiTake: Share of freehold, all on one level, its own door and private sun-trap courtyard a moment from the marina for £150,000 — genuinely good value, but the whole flat is only 259 square feet and there is no parking.

parking.note: No parking is mentioned anywhere in the particulars, so this is kerbside only. Morton Road sits in central Exmouth by the seafront and marina, which is inside the area Devon County Council has covered with its residents’ parking permit scheme since 2023, run through MiPermit at roughly £35 a year for a first band A permit — cheap and realistically obtainable if this address falls inside a live zone. The catch is that the zones were drawn street by street and the seafront end of town carries the heaviest summer visitor pressure in Exmouth, so a permit buys priority, not a reserved bay. Confirm the zone for this exact address with Devon County Council before treating it as solved. The Queen’s Drive and Estuary car parks are a short walk but are priced for tourists; East Devon District Council does sell a virtual monthly town permit for its Exmouth car parks as a fallback.

properties.title: Littleham Road, Exmouth (architect-designed bungalow down a private lane, garage/workshop plus parking for two, no chain)

flags.text: HAS PARKING (2 cars on the lane + single garage with power and light)
GARAGE/WORKSHOP WITH ITS OWN STORE AREA
SECLUDED — PRIVATE LANE, WALLED COURTYARD GARDEN
TENURE NOT STATED — AGENT ASKS YOU TO CONFIRM

properties.body: An architect-designed bungalow of around 2000, tucked down a private lane behind the Cranford Avenue shopping parade in Exmouth. It was built to a high standard with a generous glazed frontage, and runs as an open-plan kitchen with a modern fitted range of units and a Worcester combi boiler, a living space, one bedroom of 12’6" x 8’4", and a stylish modern bathroom of 9’11" x 12’6" with a large shower cubicle, chrome grab rails and a heated towel rail. Outside, the agent singles the garden out for special note: reached through an archway, enclosed by brick boundaries, laid to several sunny paved areas for outside entertaining, with a timber shed, solar lighting and an outside tap. From the private lane there is parking for approximately two cars plus a single garage of 12’7" x 10’3" with an up-and-over door, power and light, and an additional store area in front of it. uPVC double glazing throughout, gas central heating, council tax band A, no onward chain. Pennys have not stated the tenure and explicitly ask buyers to confirm freehold or leasehold with them.
properties.why: Almost everything on the practical checklist is ticked here — it is a bungalow so it is entirely on one level and passes the long-term stairs test outright, it has real parking plus a powered and lit garage that would work as a workshop, the garden is walled and private, and it sits down its own lane rather than on an estate road, which suits the preference for somewhere a bit more tucked away. The bathroom already has grab rails fitted, which is telling about how it has been lived in. The thing that stops it scoring higher is simple arithmetic: £250,000 for one bedroom. That is the exact shape of purchase Bro 3 marks down hardest, and it leaves no room to grow. It is also a 2000 build, so the character is in the architecture and the glazing rather than in beams and thatch. Worth a look if a low-maintenance, one-level, workshop-equipped base matters more than bedroom count — and the unstated tenure needs answering first, because for a bungalow it really ought to be freehold.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A one-off architect-designed bungalow from around 2000 hidden down a private lane behind a shopping parade — a big glazed frontage and a walled courtyard, nothing like the housing either side of it.

properties.aiTake: Ticks the practical boxes almost completely — one level, real parking, a powered garage/workshop and a private walled garden down its own lane — but £250,000 buys just one bedroom here, and the agent has not even said whether it is freehold.

parking.note: Parking for approximately two cars on the private lane, plus a single garage of 12’7" x 10’3" with an up-and-over door, power and light, and an extra store area in front of it. The powered garage is the useful part — it is described as a garage/workshop and would take a bike bench or a project without needing anything doing to it.

properties.title: Mill Street, Sidmouth (freehold town-centre cottage with level access — garage offered separately)

flags.text: LEVEL ACCESS — NO STEPS UP FROM THE STREET
SHORT STROLL TO THE ESPLANADE AND SEAFRONT
NO PARKING INCLUDED IN THE PRICE
VERY THIN LISTING — ALMOST NO DETAIL GIVEN

properties.body: A one-bedroom freehold cottage on Mill Street in the centre of Sidmouth, a short walk from the town centre shops, the esplanade and the seafront. The agent makes a point of the level access — no steps up from the street — which matters for the long-term single-level test. Council tax band A. The listing is remarkably thin: two sentences of description and nothing on room sizes, condition, heating, outside space or what the cottage actually contains beyond the photographs and a single floorplan. The one concrete extra is that a town-centre garage is offered alongside it for a further £40,000, which would take the real total to £230,000 if you wanted parking.
properties.why: Freehold at £190,000 in the middle of a coastal town, on the level, is a decent starting point, and the option to buy a town-centre garage — a genuinely scarce thing in Sidmouth — is more than most flats at this price can offer. But the £40,000 asked for it is a lot, and buying both puts you at £230,000 for a one-bedroom cottage, which is where Bro 3’s "too expensive for what it is" test starts to bite. The bigger problem is how little the agent has said. Two sentences is not enough to judge condition, heating or outside space, and for a town-centre cottage of unstated age those are exactly the things that decide whether this is a bargain or a project. Worth a call to the agent before a viewing, purely to find out what is actually being sold.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A separately purchasable town-centre garage — a rare commodity in Sidmouth, where the main car park has gone pay-and-display and the reserved-permit list is closed.

properties.aiTake: Freehold, level-access and walkable to the seafront for £190,000 is a fair Sidmouth entry point, but it is one bedroom, the parking costs another £40,000, and the two-sentence listing gives you almost nothing to judge it on.

parking.note: No parking is included at the asking price — the agent instead offers a town-centre garage as a separate £40,000 purchase, which tells you how tight parking is here. Researching the alternatives confirms it: the Mill Street car park immediately by the cottage was converted by East Devon District Council from permit-holder use to public pay-and-display (£1 per hour for the first two hours, £3 for four hours), and the reserved-space permit that used to cover it cost £2,000 a year including VAT, with a 25 per cent discount for Sidmouth council-tax payers — and that application process is now closed, so it is not currently available to a new owner. Devon County Council does run residents’ on-street permits for the Sidmouth zones, so that is the first thing to check with them for this specific address; if it does not qualify, the £40,000 garage stops being an optional extra and becomes the realistic answer.

properties.title: Church Street, Sidford (Grade II listed thatched cottage, freehold, no onward chain)

flags.text: NO PARKING (long-stay car park on the same street)
ONLY 1 BEDROOM — AND IT IS UPSTAIRS
FRONTS DIRECTLY ONTO THE ROAD — PATIO GARDEN ONLY

properties.body: A one-bedroom Grade II listed thatched cottage on Church Street in Sidford, the village that sits immediately inland of Sidmouth. The photographs show the real thing: a whitewashed cob elevation under a well-kept thatch that runs on into the attached neighbour, small-paned windows, a date stone set into the front wall and a low local-stone boundary wall onto the pavement. Inside there is a spacious characterful living room, a galley kitchen, and upstairs a generously proportioned double bedroom with a large bathroom. It has gas central heating, which is not a given in a cottage of this age, and a patio area outside for sitting out. Freehold, council tax band B, and offered with no onward chain. There is no garden beyond the patio and no parking of its own — the cottage fronts straight onto the street.
properties.why: This is the closest thing this sweep found to what Jesse actually says he wants: a genuinely thatched, genuinely listed cottage, freehold, chain free, and at £165,000 it lands under his real £170,000 target rather than merely under the £300,000 ceiling. Character at this price normally comes with a catch, and here the catches are honest ones — it is one bedroom, that bedroom is up the stairs, there is no garden to speak of, and the front door opens onto a road rather than a lane. Parking is the obvious gap, but it is a softer gap than usual because Sidford’s long-stay car park is on this same street. The real trade is location: Sidford is further east than the usual hunting ground, so it is a longer run to both brothers and to Exmouth than anything in Woodbury or East Budleigh, and there is no train station nearby. Worth seeing on character and price alone, with eyes open about the thatch and listed-building maintenance bill.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A date stone set into the front elevation and a thatch that runs continuously into the attached neighbour — an 18th-century village cottage that has survived largely intact, with a blue plaque on the pair next door.

properties.aiTake: A real thatched, Grade II listed, freehold cottage at £165,000 with no chain — exactly Jesse’s stated taste and under his actual target — held back by one upstairs bedroom, no parking of its own, a roadside frontage and a location further east than the rest of the search.

parking.note: The cottage has no parking of its own and fronts straight onto Church Street, so there is nothing to pull onto. The saving grace is unusually specific: East Devon District Council runs a long-stay car park called Church Street car park in Sidford, on this same street, and up to 15 of its spaces are let as reserved annual spaces at roughly £300 per space per year. That is a rentable, named, walkable answer rather than a vague "there is a car park nearby" — but it is a rental, not an asset, and the reserved spaces are a fixed and small number, so check availability with EDDC (01404 516551) before assuming one is obtainable. Devon County Council’s residents’ permit scheme covers the Sidmouth zones rather than Sidford, so an on-street permit is unlikely to be the route here.

properties.title: Burnt House Barn, Northmostown, near Sidmouth (Grade II thatched cob barn with full planning consent for a 3-bed conversion)

flags.text: GRADE II LISTED COB & THATCHED BARN
HAS PARKING (courtyard driveway + attached garage in the consented plans)
AONB — RURAL HAMLET, SURROUNDED BY COUNTRYSIDE
AT THE TOP OF BUDGET — AND THIS IS ONLY THE SHELL
CONVERSION COST ON TOP — NOT HABITABLE AS IT STANDS
ALL 3 BEDROOMS UPSTAIRS IN THE CONSENTED PLANS

properties.body: A Grade II listed cob and thatched barn in the hamlet of Northmostown, sold as a shell with detailed planning permission already granted by East Devon District Council on 18 September 2025 (ref 25/1773/FUL) to remove an attached Nissen hut and convert the barn into a single three-bedroom dwelling with parking area and landscaping. The plot runs to roughly 0.2 acres. The architect's drawings included in the listing show, at ground level, an entrance into a vaulted living room open to the roof, then dining room, kitchen, utility/boot room and a shower room, with an attached outbuilding/garage at the western end and a courtyard driveway and turning area in front. Upstairs are a mezzanine looking down into the living room, bedroom 1 (11.51 sq m, vaulted), bedroom 2 (7.50 sq m), an office/third bedroom, a bathroom and an en-suite. The elevations specify a new water reed thatch and lime render. Steps rise from the courtyard to a garden overlooking fields. Services are proposed rather than connected — heating by air source heat pump or oil boiler, and a new sewage treatment plant. Standard and ultrafast broadband are available. Northmostown sits about 3.5 miles from Sidmouth and 4.7 from Budleigh Salterton, with Otterton, East Budleigh and Colaton Raleigh all nearby, and Exeter about 14 miles away.
properties.why: This is the closest thing to Jesse's stated ideal that has come up in months — a genuinely characterful thatched, listed building, in a quiet rural hamlet surrounded by countryside rather than in a village centre, with its own garden, courtyard parking and an attached garage, and a very short hop to Otterton and East Budleigh where family already are. The planning risk is already taken: consent is granted and current, which is what usually kills barn conversions at this price. The catch is the money. £300,000 is an opening figure for a shell, and a listed cob-and-thatch conversion done to consent — new thatch, lime render, heat pump, treatment plant, full fit-out — realistically adds £250,000 or more on top, plus £27,654 of Community Infrastructure Levy unless the self-build exemption applies (it does if you live there three years). Against a £170,000 target this is in a different league entirely, and there would be a year or more of living somewhere else while it is built. Worth noting too that the consented layout puts all three bedrooms upstairs, with only a shower room downstairs — the plans could in principle be reworked for a ground-floor bedroom, but on a listed building that means a fresh listed building consent, not a pen stroke.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A Grade II listed cob-and-thatch agricultural barn sold as a blank canvas with consent already in hand — you get to design the inside of a listed building rather than inherit someone else's choices, and the consented scheme includes a vaulted living room open to the roof with a mezzanine above it.

properties.aiTake: Thatched, listed, rural, private, with garage, garden and consent already granted — on character it is the best fit yet, but £300,000 buys only the shell and the finished cost lands somewhere near double Jesse's ceiling.

parking.note: The consented plans show a courtyard driveway and turning area directly in front of the barn plus an attached outbuilding/garage at the western end, with the existing 3.0m-wide vehicle access off the lane retained. Parking is therefore off-road, on the plot and generous by the standards of anything else on this list — but it exists on paper rather than on the ground today, so it arrives only when the conversion is built out.

properties.title: North Street, Exmouth (ground-floor apartment in the courtyard and gardens of a historic manor house, share of freehold)

flags.text: GROUND FLOOR — ALL ON ONE LEVEL
SHARE OF FREEHOLD — NO GROUND RENT
SET IN THE COURTYARD & GARDENS OF A HISTORIC MANOR HOUSE
OWN PRIVATE 3-TIERED TERRACE GARDEN WITH APPLE & HOLLY TREES
LEVEL WALK TO TOWN, STATION & SEAFRONT

properties.body: A self-contained ground-floor apartment tucked into the courtyard and gardens of a historic old manor house, right in the middle of Exmouth town centre. Inside it has been repainted throughout with new vinyl flooring to the hallway and bathroom, and comprises a bright dual-aspect kitchen/living room looking out over both the garden and the courtyard, one spacious double bedroom, a hallway with a tall storage cupboard, and a bathroom with a shower over the bath and further storage. Outside, it has its own private three-tiered terrace garden with mature apple and holly trees, plus access to a communal drying area and a large shed usable for bikes or garden furniture. The agent stresses how quiet the setting is despite the central location. It carries a share of the freehold with no ground rent payable and a 2026 service charge of £854.51. No onward chain. EPC E, council tax band A. The agent quotes an estimated rental value of about £900 per calendar month.
properties.why: At £132,500 this is comfortably the cheapest characterful thing on the list, and it is a rare combination: entirely on one level, share of freehold with no ground rent, a genuinely private garden of its own rather than a communal lawn, and a setting in the grounds of an old manor house that is far more interesting than the price suggests. Everything — town, railway station, seafront — is a level walk. The two real limits are that it is a one-bedroom flat, which rules out a child having a room, and that no parking comes with it in the heart of the town centre. Against Jesse's £170,000 target it leaves a lot of headroom, so it reads more as a cheap, low-risk, easily-let base than as a forever home.

checklist.uniqueFeature: The flat sits inside the walled courtyard and gardens of a historic manor house in the middle of the town — and comes with its own three-tiered terrace garden of mature apple and holly trees, which is not something a £132,500 town-centre flat normally has.

properties.aiTake: Cheap, all on one level, share of freehold, and a private orchard-ish garden in a manor house courtyard — held back by being a one-bedroom with no parking of its own.

parking.note: The listing offers no parking at all, and North Street sits in the middle of Exmouth town centre where kerbside space is time-limited and enforced 8am to 6pm Monday to Saturday. Worth knowing that North Street was inside the wider area consulted on for Exmouth's residents' parking scheme, but the zones that actually went live cover The Colonies, St Andrews Road, part of Albion Hill and Carter Avenue — not North Street — so there is currently no residents' permit to buy for this address. The realistic answer is a season permit in an East Devon District Council long-stay car park: Imperial Road Recreation Ground is the main long-stay option in the town at roughly 240 spaces and is about a five-minute walk away, and the Manor Road/Magnolia area car parks are closer still. The listing does note a large shed on site suitable for bikes, which matters more here than it usually would.

properties.title: Trefusis Terrace, Exmouth (2-bed lower-ground-floor apartment with its own garage, no chain)

flags.text: FEATURE FIREPLACE IN THE LIVING ROOM
LEASEHOLD — TERM NOT STATED, ASK AGENT
LOWER GROUND FLOOR — STEPS DOWN FROM STREET LEVEL

properties.body: A spacious two-bedroom lower-ground-floor apartment on Trefusis Terrace, a Victorian terrace a short walk from Exmouth seafront and the Maer. The accommodation runs from an entrance hall with plumbing for a washing machine into a modern kitchen with integrated appliances and a large living room with a feature fireplace, then a generous master bedroom, a second double bedroom and a modern bathroom. A garage comes with it. Offered with no onward chain. Council tax band B. Bradleys' particulars are unusually brief for a flat of this size and do not state the lease length, service charge or ground rent, nor whether any outside space comes with it.
properties.why: Two double bedrooms, a garage of its own and a position within walking distance of the seafront for £220,000 is a fair deal in Exmouth, and the feature fireplace and Victorian proportions give it a bit more warmth than the modern flats that usually sit at this price. Being lower ground floor means steps down from street level, which cuts against the long-term single-level test even though the flat itself is on one floor. The bigger issue is how little the agent has actually said: no lease length, no service charge, no ground rent and no mention of outside space, all of which need answering before it can be judged properly — a short lease in particular would change the picture entirely.
properties.aiTake: Two doubles, a garage and the seafront on the doorstep for £220,000 is decent value, but it is a lower-ground flat with no stated lease length and a listing too thin to judge properly.

parking.note: A garage is included with the flat, which is a real advantage on Trefusis Terrace — this is Victorian terraced housing close to the seafront where kerbside space is contested, particularly in summer. The particulars do not say whether the garage is on the plot or in a nearby block, so that is worth asking.

properties.title: Mount Pleasant Avenue, Exmouth (2-bed ground-floor apartment with its own private driveway)

flags.text: GROUND FLOOR — ALL ON ONE LEVEL
LEASEHOLD — TERM NOT STATED, ASK AGENT
NORTH SIDE OF TOWN — NOT WALKABLE TO THE SEAFRONT

properties.body: A two-bedroom ground-floor apartment on Mount Pleasant Avenue on the northern side of Exmouth, running to 755 sq ft. The floorplan shows a 17ft 2in x 14ft 6in sitting room, a separate kitchen, two genuine double bedrooms (both 14ft 11in long) off a central hallway, a shower room and a separate WC. It comes with a private driveway giving off-road parking. Bradleys describe it as spacious and well presented with a modern kitchen and contemporary shower room. The particulars are brief and do not state the lease length, service charge, ground rent or whether any garden comes with it.
properties.why: 755 sq ft entirely on one level with two proper doubles and its own driveway for £210,000 is sensible, practical value, and off-road parking attached to a ground-floor flat is genuinely useful given how often that is the missing piece on this list. It is also completely plain — a modern flat with no character to speak of, which is exactly the profile that has scored badly with the family before. Mount Pleasant Avenue is a mile and a half north of the seafront, so this is an Exmouth address rather than a coastal one, and as with the Trefusis Terrace flat from the same agent the listing withholds the lease length and service charge, which need checking before it means anything.
properties.aiTake: A big, sensible, entirely single-level two-double flat with its own driveway at a fair price — but plain, garden-less and with the lease length left unstated.

parking.note: A private driveway providing off-road parking comes with the flat, which is unusual for an apartment at this price and removes any dependence on kerbside space. Mount Pleasant Avenue is a residential road on the northern side of Exmouth and sits outside the residents' permit zones that went live in the town, so visitor parking on the street should also be straightforward.

properties.title: Lyndhurst Road, Exmouth (ground-floor 2-bed flat that owns the freehold of the building, own rear garden)

flags.text: GROUND FLOOR — ALL ON ONE LEVEL
OWNS THE FREEHOLD TO THE BUILDING
LEVEL WALK TO TOWN, STATION & SEAFRONT

properties.body: A bay-fronted Edwardian terrace on Lyndhurst Road, split into two flats, with this one occupying the whole ground floor. Accommodation is an entrance hall, a bay-fronted sitting room that doubles as bedroom 2 (17ft into the bay), a separate living/dining room, fitted kitchen, lean-to utility, master bedroom and a bathroom with shower over the bath. Gas central heating and uPVC double glazing throughout. Outside there is a good-sized enclosed rear garden — shingle by the house, then lawn, a raised artificial-grass deck, shrub borders, brick and timber-fenced boundaries and a pedestrian gate to the rear. The unusual bit is the tenure: the flat is leasehold on a 199-year lease granted 31 January 2018, but it also owns the freehold of the whole building, which contains just one other flat on the first floor. In practice that means you control the building rather than answering to a landlord or a managing agent.
properties.why: Sub-£200k, genuinely all on one level, with its own private garden and effective control of the freehold — that combination almost never appears at this price around Exmouth. It is a level walk to the town centre, the railway station and Phear Park, and the seafront is a manageable stroll. The Edwardian bay and brick frontage give it more character than most flats on the list. The catch is parking: nothing off-road, and Lyndhurst Road sits inside Exmouth’s residents’ permit machinery, so that is the thing to pin down before offering.

checklist.uniqueFeature: The flat owns the freehold to the entire building (only one other flat above) on top of a 199-year lease — freehold-like control on a £185,000 ground-floor flat.

properties.aiTake: Cheap, entirely ground-floor, with its own garden and effective ownership of the building — the only real gap is off-road parking.

parking.note: No off-road parking is claimed anywhere on the listing. The front is a small gravelled forecourt behind a low brick wall with a path to the door — there is no dropped kerb visible in the photos, so do not assume you could park a car on it without applying for one. Researching the street: Devon County Council’s 2023 Exmouth traffic orders put ‘No Waiting At Any Time’ on specified lengths of Lyndhurst Road, and a later amendment order proposes Residents Parking (Zonal), 8am–8pm, Zone D on specified lengths of the same road. So a resident permit looks obtainable, but which side and which stretch matters a lot here — ask Devon County Council (or the agent) exactly which length of Lyndhurst Road this address falls on before assuming a permit gets you a space near the door. As a fallback, East Devon District Council sells a virtual monthly town permit valid in its Exmouth pay-and-display car parks, and Phear Park is a couple of minutes away.

properties.title: Clinton Square, Exmouth (1-bed all on one level, own private entrance, courtyard garden and log burner)

flags.text: IN BUDGET — WELL UNDER JESSE’S £170K TARGET
OWN PRIVATE ENTRANCE — NO COMMUNAL HALL
LEASEHOLD — TERM NOT STATED, ASK AGENT

properties.body: A one-bedroom property tucked into Clinton Square, moments from Exmouth town centre and the seafront. The floor plan confirms it is entirely ground floor: living room (12ft 6in x 12ft 5in) with a log burner, a shower room, a kitchen/diner (12ft 6in x 10ft 2in) and a double bedroom of the same size at the rear. It has its own private front door rather than a shared communal hallway, and a sunlit private rear courtyard. Chain-free. Bradleys’ particulars are unusually thin — the tenure is stated as leasehold but no lease length, ground rent or service charge figure is given, so those are the first three questions to ask.
properties.why: The cheapest thing on the list in a genuinely good spot — town centre and seafront both on the doorstep, all on one level, with its own front door, its own outdoor space and a wood burner for character. At £140,000 it is £30k below Jesse’s real target, which leaves room for the unknowns. It is only one bedroom and there is no parking, and the missing lease detail is a real gap rather than a formality — a short lease would change the picture completely.

checklist.uniqueFeature: Its own private street entrance and enclosed courtyard on a £140,000 flat a few minutes from Exmouth seafront — plus a working log burner.

properties.aiTake: Cheapest genuinely liveable thing on the list — one level, own front door, own courtyard, log burner — held back by one bedroom, no parking and an unstated lease.

parking.note: No parking is mentioned in the particulars at all. Researching it: Devon County Council’s 2023 Exmouth parking orders put ‘No Waiting At Any Time’ on specified lengths of Clinton Square itself, so the kerb directly outside is likely to be restricted rather than a free-for-all. The surrounding central streets fall inside Exmouth’s residents’ parking zones (introduced 2023, now five zones with resident, visitor, business and blue-badge permit types), so a resident permit is the realistic route — but this is the busiest, most tourist-pressured part of town in summer and a permit gives priority, not a reserved bay. East Devon District Council’s Imperial Road and Estuary car parks are both a short walk away, and EDDC sells a virtual monthly town permit for its car parks. Confirm with Devon County Council which zone this address qualifies for before treating parking as solved.

properties.title: North Street, Ottery St Mary (2-bed brick-and-flint cottage, log burner, one of the largest gardens in the area, plus a studio)

flags.text: PERIOD COTTAGE — EXPOSED BEAMS & TIMBER FLOOR
ONE OF THE LARGEST GARDENS IN THE AREA

properties.body: A brick-and-flint mid-terrace cottage fronting straight onto the pavement on North Street, within walking distance of Ottery St Mary town centre and inside the King’s School catchment. Downstairs is a large sitting/dining room with exposed beams and an exposed timber floor, a timber window seat, and a brick fireplace housing a log burner; the kitchen opens onto a covered veranda. Upstairs are two bedrooms and a family bathroom — the front bedroom has a cast-iron fireplace and original stripped-pine cupboard doors. The garden is the headline: Hall & Scott describe it as one of the largest in the area, with a good-sized paved patio, a small deck with a whitewashed wall surround, and lawn with flower borders. At the far end is a studio (2.9m x 2.2m) with light and power laid on, opening onto its own decked patio. Chain-free.
properties.why: This is the sort of thing Bro 3 has rated well before — real character, a genuinely finished outbuilding that could work as a studio or guest space, and a garden well out of proportion to the price. The exposed beams, timber floor and working log burner are the real deal rather than a stripped-back modernisation. The downsides, plainly: it is inland, so the coast checklist item is a straight no, and it fronts the pavement with no parking mentioned anywhere. Ottery is roughly 25 minutes from Exmouth and closer to the Otterton side, so it is a compromise on location rather than a disqualification.

checklist.uniqueFeature: A separate studio at the bottom of the garden with light and power already laid on, opening onto its own decked patio.

properties.aiTake: Genuine cottage character, a log burner and an outsized garden with a finished studio — undercut by being inland with no parking and no realistic ground-floor bedroom.

parking.note: The particulars do not mention parking at all, and the front elevation photo shows the cottage opening straight onto the pavement with no forecourt, so on-street is the working assumption. Researching Ottery: Devon County Council has not introduced a residents’ permit scheme here, so unrestricted on-street stretches are simply first-come-first-served — better than a permit lottery in some ways, worse in that you have no priority at all. East Devon District Council’s Brook Street car park is in the centre of town a few minutes’ walk away (charges 08:00–18:00 Monday–Saturday, from 50p for 30 minutes, free on Sundays), and EDDC’s virtual monthly town permit covers Ottery St Mary for its car parks. The Sainsbury’s car park on Hind Street also offers monthly parking from around £65. One thing genuinely worth asking the agent given how long the garden is: whether there is any rear vehicular access to the bottom of the plot, because on a garden that size it would be the obvious place to create a space.
